course_map.title: Finite prefixes and compatible sequences
course_map.worked_example_capability: Test compatibility of successive finite addresses
course_map.assessment_target: Test compatibility of successive finite addresses

teaching_anchor.bridge_to_teach: A depth-d address is a residue modulo 3^d in each of three coordinates. The bonding map reduces modulo 3^d. Start with a single coordinate before taking triples; store digit order from least significant first. Balanced digits -1,0,1 are converted to residues with ordinary modular arithmetic.

guided_practice.task_and_answer: Digits (0,1,-1,0,1) give (0,3,21,75,75); check each reduction. A proposed list (1,8) at moduli (3,9) fails because 8 mod3=2. Retain the incompatible proposal with its failed reduction.

diagnostic.task_and_answer: Different integer representatives can be the same residue: -2=7 mod9. Compatibility concerns reduction, not increasing real magnitude. Five prefixes do not fix an unspecified infinite continuation.

course_map.title: A different meaning of closeness
course_map.worked_example_capability: Compare real distance with common-prefix address closeness
course_map.assessment_target: Compare real distance with common-prefix address closeness

teaching_anchor.bridge_to_teach: Define address distance 3^-k when two distinct addresses first differ after k shared low-order ternary digits; identical addresses have distance zero. Contrast with ordinary real distance. In triples, declare the maximum coordinate address distance. Never infer an exact history from a rounded real image.

worked_example.task_and_answer: Integers 1 and 28 differ by 27=3^3, so address distance is 1/27 while real distance is 27. Integers 1 and 2 have address distance 1 and real distance 1.

guided_practice.task_and_answer: 4 and 13 differ by 9, so address distance is 1/9 and real distance is 9. In triples (1,4,0) and (28,13,0), the maximum coordinate address distance is 1/9. State which distance is being compared.

diagnostic.task_and_answer: A small real difference and a long common address prefix are different conditions. For the later renderer, histories (1,-1,-1,...) and (0,1,1,...) have equal real images but disagree modulo3 at depth1.

course_map.title: The ternary inverse limit
course_map.worked_example_capability: Construct finite approximations to the source address object
course_map.assessment_target: Construct finite approximations to the source address object

teaching_anchor.bridge_to_teach: Define the inverse limit as the set of all compatible sequences, not merely the last residue in a finite list. A complete digit rule specifies an infinite example; a finite prefix plus an unresolved continuation remains partial. Use three independent coordinate sequences for Z_3^3.

worked_example.task_and_answer: Take all balanced digits +1. The depth-d integer representative is a_d=(3^d-1)/2, giving 1,4,13,40 at d=1..4. Reduction is compatible because a_(d+1)-a_d=3^d. A triple of this sequence, all-zero digits and all-minus-one digits is a specified inverse-limit point.

guided_practice.task_and_answer: All digits -1 give -1,-4,-13,-40, or residues 2,5,14,41. Check reduction and distinguish the stored digit history from these nonnegative representatives. A finite prefix admits three choices for its next digit in each coordinate, hence 27 next triples.

diagnostic.task_and_answer: A finite truncation does not prove the digits eventually vanish. Keep a specified tail rule when one exists and unresolved continuation when it does not. Inverse-limit existence here follows the explicit compatibility construction; no arbitrary operator has yet been defined.

teaching_anchor.bridge_to_teach: C22-TAIL-EX1: teach S_N=r+...+r^N by subtracting r S_N from S_N; for r not equal to1, S_N=r(1-r^N)/(1-r). The infinite absolute-tail bound requires |r|<1. Then apply the idea to z_N=(1/2)sum_(j=1)^N 3^-j u_j and r_N=B z_N, with bounded balanced digits and a declared length-valued B.

worked_example.task_and_answer: For d_j=2^-j, S_N=1-2^-N and the tail is 2^-N. Epsilon=0.01 requires N=7 because 1/128<=0.01<1/64. In M18, each normalized coordinate tail is <=1/(4*3^N). Thus normalized tolerance 1/1000 requires N=6, not5. For B=diag(2,3,4) LU, the physical infinity-norm tail is <=1/3^N LU.

guided_practice.task_and_answer: C22-TAIL-P1: epsilon=1/32 permits N=5. For B=diag(2,3,4) LU and physical infinity-norm tolerance 1/1000 LU, N=7 is needed because 1/2187<=1/1000<1/729. Histories (1,-1,-1,...) and (0,1,1,...) both render normalized 1/12: (1/2)(1/3-1/6)=(1/2)(1/6). Retain both distinct histories.

diagnostic.task_and_answer: C22-TAIL-D1: r=1 gives growing partial sums and no convergent geometric tail. A signed cancellation is not an absolute bound. For general B use a stated induced norm, e.g. ||B||_infinity/(4*3^N); do not report a dimensionless coordinate bound as a physical vector bound or delete the tail history.

course_map.title: Cylinder observations
course_map.worked_example_capability: Explain an observation that depends on only a finite prefix
course_map.assessment_target: Explain an observation that depends on only a finite prefix

teaching_anchor.bridge_to_teach: A cylinder observation depends only on a declared finite prefix. Define f_d on residues and pull it to depth d+1 by composition with reduction. Such an observation leaves all finer coordinates available; equal observations do not identify equal addresses.

worked_example.task_and_answer: Let f_1(a)=1 when a mod3=1, else0. At depth2 the residues 1,4,7 all give1. At depth3 every extension a+9k of these depth2 residues has the same value. This is a finite-prefix observable, not a measurement of the entire history.

guided_practice.task_and_answer: Let g_2(a)=a mod9. The depth3 addresses 7,16,25 all give7, but their third digits differ. Preserve the three address labels alongside the shared g value. For triples apply g to the first coordinate with the other two retained.

diagnostic.task_and_answer: If a proposed depth3 observation reads the third digit, it cannot be claimed to depend only on depth1. State the smallest prefix it actually uses and retain the unresolved finer sectors.

course_map.title: Retained-detail filtrations
course_map.worked_example_capability: Reconstruct successive levels without dropping detail sectors
course_map.assessment_target: Reconstruct successive levels without dropping detail sectors

teaching_anchor.bridge_to_teach: Teach conditional averaging and detail on four explicit cells before the infinite notation. P0 replaces all entries by their mean; P1 replaces each adjacent pair by its mean. Set Q0=P1-P0 and Q1=I-P1. Show nesting P0 P1=P0, orthogonality and reconstruction. This finite identity alone is not an infinite operator-domain theorem.

worked_example.task_and_answer: For v=(1,3,5,7), P0 v=(4,4,4,4), Q0 v=(-2,-2,2,2), Q1 v=(-1,1,-1,1). Their sum is v. Supply the 4x4 matrices and check each is an orthogonal projector and mixed products vanish.

guided_practice.task_and_answer: For v=(2,0,6,4), mean=(3,3,3,3), between-pair detail=(-2,-2,2,2), within-pair detail=(1,-1,1,-1). Recover P1 v=(1,1,5,5) and then v from all pieces. Keep zero detail coordinates if present.

diagnostic.task_and_answer: Saving just P0 v loses both detail sectors. The identity I=P0+sum Qn in an infinite space requires the convergence mode and limiting space; a finite projector calculation supplies a bridge, not those missing hypotheses.

course_map.title: Infinite objects and operator domains
course_map.worked_example_capability: Identify what must be supplied before an infinite operator is meaningful
course_map.assessment_target: Identify what must be supplied before an infinite operator is meaningful

teaching_anchor.bridge_to_teach: An infinite operator needs a space, norm or topology, domain, action and convergence rules. On l2(N>=1), define D x=(n x_n) with domain sum n^2 |x_n|^2 finite. Explain this as a weighted convergence test before discussing any source operator. Keep this example separate from unspecified archival operators.

worked_example.task_and_answer: x_n=1/n belongs to l2 because sum1/n^2 converges (compare blocks [2^k,2^(k+1)) with bound2^-k). But D x=(1,1,...) is not in l2, so x is outside the domain of D. Every finite truncation is in the domain; that does not put the limit in it.

guided_practice.task_and_answer: x_n=1/n^2 is in the domain because sum n^2/n^4=sum1/n^2 converges. D x=1/n is in l2. For a source claim, list required carrier, domain, action, inner product and convergence mode; mark any absent item not supplied.

diagnostic.task_and_answer: A convergent real renderer does not establish boundedness or self-adjointness of every operator on histories. Preserve the ordered pair of exact history and real image, operator-domain assumptions and all detail sectors in the capstone.

source_scope.address: A_d=(Z/3^d Z)^3 with reduction bonding maps. Balanced least-significant-first digits define finite residue histories; a full infinite rule or unresolved continuation is retained.
source_scope.paired_object: The object is the ordered pair (exact compatible 3-adic history, convergent real image). Distinct balanced endpoint histories (1,-1,-1,...) and (0,1,1,...) both render normalized 1/12. No injectivity of the real renderer is claimed.
source_scope.tail: Per normalized coordinate, absolute tail <=1/(4*3^N). For physical r=Bz, use the declared matrix norm and units; infinity norm bound ||B||_infinity/(4*3^N). Signed partial sums, full digit rule, prefix depth and bound all remain available.
source_scope.detail: The finite mean/pair/detail example checks P0+Q0+Q1=I and retains every vector. An infinite filtration also needs an ambient space and convergence mode; any product rule needs the actual conditional-expectation hypotheses noted in AUD-006.
source_scope.domains: The explicitly defined unbounded diagonal operator on l2 is a domain exercise only. It is not a substitute for an unloaded archival history operator.

lessons.bridge_to_teach: A depth-d address is a residue modulo 3^d in each of three coordinates. The bonding map reduces modulo 3^d. Start with a single coordinate before taking triples; store digit order from least significant first. Balanced digits -1,0,1 are converted to residues with ordinary modular arithmetic.

guided_practice.task_and_answer: Digits (0,1,-1,0,1) give (0,3,21,75,75); check each reduction. A proposed list (1,8) at moduli (3,9) fails because 8 mod3=2. Retain the incompatible proposal with its failed reduction.

diagnostic.task_and_answer: Different integer representatives can be the same residue: -2=7 mod9. Compatibility concerns reduction, not increasing real magnitude. Five prefixes do not fix an unspecified infinite continuation.

lessons.bridge_to_teach: Define address distance 3^-k when two distinct addresses first differ after k shared low-order ternary digits; identical addresses have distance zero. Contrast with ordinary real distance. In triples, declare the maximum coordinate address distance. Never infer an exact history from a rounded real image.

worked_example.task_and_answer: Integers 1 and 28 differ by 27=3^3, so address distance is 1/27 while real distance is 27. Integers 1 and 2 have address distance 1 and real distance 1.

guided_practice.task_and_answer: 4 and 13 differ by 9, so address distance is 1/9 and real distance is 9. In triples (1,4,0) and (28,13,0), the maximum coordinate address distance is 1/9. State which distance is being compared.

diagnostic.task_and_answer: A small real difference and a long common address prefix are different conditions. For the later renderer, histories (1,-1,-1,...) and (0,1,1,...) have equal real images but disagree modulo3 at depth1.

lessons.bridge_to_teach: Define the inverse limit as the set of all compatible sequences, not merely the last residue in a finite list. A complete digit rule specifies an infinite example; a finite prefix plus an unresolved continuation remains partial. Use three independent coordinate sequences for Z_3^3.

worked_example.task_and_answer: Take all balanced digits +1. The depth-d integer representative is a_d=(3^d-1)/2, giving 1,4,13,40 at d=1..4. Reduction is compatible because a_(d+1)-a_d=3^d. A triple of this sequence, all-zero digits and all-minus-one digits is a specified inverse-limit point.

guided_practice.task_and_answer: All digits -1 give -1,-4,-13,-40, or residues 2,5,14,41. Check reduction and distinguish the stored digit history from these nonnegative representatives. A finite prefix admits three choices for its next digit in each coordinate, hence 27 next triples.

diagnostic.task_and_answer: A finite truncation does not prove the digits eventually vanish. Keep a specified tail rule when one exists and unresolved continuation when it does not. Inverse-limit existence here follows the explicit compatibility construction; no arbitrary operator has yet been defined.

lessons.bridge_to_teach: C22-TAIL-EX1: teach S_N=r+...+r^N by subtracting r S_N from S_N; for r not equal to1, S_N=r(1-r^N)/(1-r). The infinite absolute-tail bound requires |r|<1. Then apply the idea to z_N=(1/2)sum_(j=1)^N 3^-j u_j and r_N=B z_N, with bounded balanced digits and a declared length-valued B.

worked_example.task_and_answer: For d_j=2^-j, S_N=1-2^-N and the tail is 2^-N. Epsilon=0.01 requires N=7 because 1/128<=0.01<1/64. In M18, each normalized coordinate tail is <=1/(4*3^N). Thus normalized tolerance 1/1000 requires N=6, not5. For B=diag(2,3,4) LU, the physical infinity-norm tail is <=1/3^N LU.

guided_practice.task_and_answer: C22-TAIL-P1: epsilon=1/32 permits N=5. For B=diag(2,3,4) LU and physical infinity-norm tolerance 1/1000 LU, N=7 is needed because 1/2187<=1/1000<1/729. Histories (1,-1,-1,...) and (0,1,1,...) both render normalized 1/12: (1/2)(1/3-1/6)=(1/2)(1/6). Retain both distinct histories.

diagnostic.task_and_answer: C22-TAIL-D1: r=1 gives growing partial sums and no convergent geometric tail. A signed cancellation is not an absolute bound. For general B use a stated induced norm, e.g. ||B||_infinity/(4*3^N); do not report a dimensionless coordinate bound as a physical vector bound or delete the tail history.

lessons.bridge_to_teach: A cylinder observation depends only on a declared finite prefix. Define f_d on residues and pull it to depth d+1 by composition with reduction. Such an observation leaves all finer coordinates available; equal observations do not identify equal addresses.

worked_example.task_and_answer: Let f_1(a)=1 when a mod3=1, else0. At depth2 the residues 1,4,7 all give1. At depth3 every extension a+9k of these depth2 residues has the same value. This is a finite-prefix observable, not a measurement of the entire history.

guided_practice.task_and_answer: Let g_2(a)=a mod9. The depth3 addresses 7,16,25 all give7, but their third digits differ. Preserve the three address labels alongside the shared g value. For triples apply g to the first coordinate with the other two retained.

diagnostic.task_and_answer: If a proposed depth3 observation reads the third digit, it cannot be claimed to depend only on depth1. State the smallest prefix it actually uses and retain the unresolved finer sectors.

lessons.bridge_to_teach: Teach conditional averaging and detail on four explicit cells before the infinite notation. P0 replaces all entries by their mean; P1 replaces each adjacent pair by its mean. Set Q0=P1-P0 and Q1=I-P1. Show nesting P0 P1=P0, orthogonality and reconstruction. This finite identity alone is not an infinite operator-domain theorem.

worked_example.task_and_answer: For v=(1,3,5,7), P0 v=(4,4,4,4), Q0 v=(-2,-2,2,2), Q1 v=(-1,1,-1,1). Their sum is v. Supply the 4x4 matrices and check each is an orthogonal projector and mixed products vanish.

guided_practice.task_and_answer: For v=(2,0,6,4), mean=(3,3,3,3), between-pair detail=(-2,-2,2,2), within-pair detail=(1,-1,1,-1). Recover P1 v=(1,1,5,5) and then v from all pieces. Keep zero detail coordinates if present.

diagnostic.task_and_answer: Saving just P0 v loses both detail sectors. The identity I=P0+sum Qn in an infinite space requires the convergence mode and limiting space; a finite projector calculation supplies a bridge, not those missing hypotheses.

lessons.bridge_to_teach: An infinite operator needs a space, norm or topology, domain, action and convergence rules. On l2(N>=1), define D x=(n x_n) with domain sum n^2 |x_n|^2 finite. Explain this as a weighted convergence test before discussing any source operator. Keep this example separate from unspecified archival operators.

worked_example.task_and_answer: x_n=1/n belongs to l2 because sum1/n^2 converges (compare blocks [2^k,2^(k+1)) with bound2^-k). But D x=(1,1,...) is not in l2, so x is outside the domain of D. Every finite truncation is in the domain; that does not put the limit in it.

guided_practice.task_and_answer: x_n=1/n^2 is in the domain because sum n^2/n^4=sum1/n^2 converges. D x=1/n is in l2. For a source claim, list required carrier, domain, action, inner product and convergence mode; mark any absent item not supplied.

diagnostic.task_and_answer: A convergent real renderer does not establish boundedness or self-adjointness of every operator on histories. Preserve the ordered pair of exact history and real image, operator-domain assumptions and all detail sectors in the capstone.
